1 1.

Vide this judgment, accused Jitender Gahlot is being acquitted of the offences punishable under Section 498A/304 B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (hereinafter referred to as 'I.P.C.') in the instant case FIR No. 48/2018 Police Station Dabri, New Delhi for the reasons mentioned below.
CASE OF PROSECUTION 2.

The case of the prosecution is that the accused Jitender Gahlot, who was married to the complainant's daughter Ms. Neelam (since deceased) on 31.07.2017, subjected her (deceased Neelam) to cruelty and harassment for not meeting his unlawful demand of dowry, including soon before her death; and that on 24.01.2018, i.e. within seven years of her marriage, at G-38, Gali no. 2,
Som Bazar Road, Rajapuri, Uttam Nagar, New Delhi, Ms. Neelam died otherwise than under normal circumstances.

3. The circumstances which put the law into motion are that on 24.01.2018, on receipt of DD no. 17 A, Sub Inspector Bikramjeet alongwith Constable Manoj reached at the spot i.e. G-38, Gali no. 2,
Som Bazar Road, Rajapuri, Uttam Nagar, New Delhi, where deceased State Vs. Jitender Gahlot Neelam was found lying dead, with a ligature mark on her neck, on a cot inside a room on the ground floor.
A chunni was also found lying on the cot.
The spot was got inspected through the Crime Team and the concerned Executive Magistrate was informed.
Mr. Puneet Kulshreshtha, the then Executive Magistrate reached at the spot and after inspecting the same, recorded the statements of the brothers of the deceased.
The dead body was shifted to Deen Dayal Upadhyay Hospital, Delhi, where the patient was declared brought dead on examination vide MLC No. 23542.
The hanging material, i.e. chunni of the deceased, was seized.
Post mortem on the dead body of the deceased was got conducted vide PM Report No. 166/18 dated 25.01.2018.
Thereafter, the body was handed over to its relatives.
The sealed exhibits handed over by the doctor after post-mortem were got deposited in the malkhana of the police station.

On 25.01.2018, the Executive Magistrate concerned recorded the statements of Mrs. Premwati, mother of the deceased as well as Ms.
Jamuna, sister of the deceased.

On 01.02.2018, the Executive Magistrate directed the SHO to take necessary action as per law, pursuant to which, the instant FIR was registered under Section 498A/304B IPC and investigation was handed over to Inspector Narender Singh.

4. During investigation, the investigating officer collected the post mortem report of the deceased Neelam, prepared the site plan, recorded the statements of witnesses, arrested accused Jitender Gahlot, and deposited the exhibits for forensic examination at FSL Rohini.

In the post mortem report, the doctor had opined the cause of death as asphyxia caused by ligature hanging by using chunni like material and kept the opinion as to manner of death pending till receipt of FSL report State Vs. Jitender Gahlot of blood and viscera.

State Vs. Jitender Gahlot DEFENCE OF THE ACCUSED 20.
In his statement recorded under Section 313 Cr.PC, vide order dated 31.08.2023, accused has denied the entire incriminating circumstances appearing in the evidence against him.
He admitted the factum of marriage between him and the deceased.

He specifically stated that neither he nor any of his relatives ever demanded any dowry or money from the deceased or her family members,
either prior to, at the time of or after the marriage with deceased Neelam.
He specifically stated that he never used to drink liquor.
He stated that on the day of the incident, he was at work, where he was informed by his neighbour about the incident and thereafter, he returned to his house.
He specifically stated that he lived a happy married life with his wife and never had any quarrel with her as has also been stated by one of his neighbours to the police.
He urged that after the death of Neelam, her relatives have manipulated/cooked up a false story against him.
He deposed that the witnesses have deposed falsely against him as they are his family members and are trying to usurp his right in the ancestral property.
Accused preferred not to lead any evidence in his defence.
21. The record has been carefully perused.

The respective submissions of Mr. Girish Kumar Manhas,

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS I. Charge for the offence punishable under Section 498A IPC State vs Jitender Gahlot on 10 November, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/170232380/
4 22.

In order to bring home the guilt of the accused in respect of State Vs. Jitender Gahlot the offence punishable under Section 498A I.P.C., the prosecution was required to prove the following:
(i) that the accused was the husband of the deceased Ms. Neelam; and (ii) that the accused had subjected the deceased Ms. Neelam to cruelty.
i) Re: Whether the accused Jitender Gahlot was the husband of the deceased Ms.
Neelam?
23.
As per the case of the prosecution, the accused Jitender Gahlot was the husband of the deceased Ms. Neelam.
PW-2 Ms. Jamuna, in her examination-in-chief dated 08.02.2019, has deposed that her sister Neelam was married to accused Jitender Gahlot one year ago at Mangol Puri, Delhi.

PW-5 Ms. Premwati, in her examination-in-chief dated 02.05.2019, has deposed that her deceased daughter Ms. Neelam was married to accused Jitender @ Jitu according to Hindu rites in the month of Ashad about one and a half years ago.
PW-6 Mr. Bablu has deposed in his examination-in-chief dated 02.07.2019 that his deceased sister Ms. Neelam was married to accused Jitender, resident of Fatehabad, Agra.
PW-7 Mr. Rajesh has deposed that in the year 2017, he had got his deceased sister Neelam married to the accused as per Hindu rites and ceremonies.
None of the said witnesses, who are mother and siblings of the deceased Ms. Neelam, has been cross-examined on the aspect of marriage between the accused Jitender Gahlot and deceased Ms. Neelam.
Further, the factum of marriage between the deceased Ms. Neelam and the accused Jitender Gahlot has not been disputed by the accused in his statement recorded under Section 313 Cr.P.C. either.

The prosecution has,
therefore, proved that the accused Jitender Gahlot was State Vs. Jitender Gahlot the husband of the deceased.
Accordingly, the first of the two ingredients, as stated above, stands established.

ii) Re: Whether the accused Jitender Gahlot had subjected the deceased Ms. Neelam to cruelty?
24.
The term "cruelty" has been defined in the Explanation1 to Section 498A I.P.C.
In the instant case, the prosecution has pressed clause (b) thereof into service.

It has been alleged that the accused Jitender Gahlot had harassed the deceased Ms. Neelam with a view to coerce her or her parents/family to meet unlawful demand for property/valuable security or on account of failure by her or her family to meet such demand.

Thus, in order to establish the charge under Section 498A IPC against the accused Jitender Gahlot, the prosecution was required to prove beyond reasonable doubt that during the subsistence of marriage accused Jitender Gahlot with the deceased Ms.
Neelam, the accused Jitender Gahlot subjected the deceased to harassment in relation to non-fulfillment of his demands for dowry.

For that purpose, the prosecution was required to prove the following:
(a) that there was an unlawful demand for any property or valuable security by the accused Jitender Gahlot from the deceased or any person related to her;
(b) that the accused Jitender Gahlot harassed the deceased Ms. Neelam; and 1 Explanation to Section 498A IPC reads as under:-

For the purpose of this section, "cruelty" means- (a)any willful conduct which is of such a nature as is likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or to cause grave injury or danger to life, limb or health (whether mental or physical) of woman; or (b)harassment of the woman where such harassment is with a view to coercing her or any person related to her to meet any unlawful demand for any property or valuable security or is on account of failure by her or any person related to her to meet such demand.

State Vs. Jitender Gahlot (c) that the harassment of the deceased was with a view either (i) to coerce her/person related to her to meet such demand or (ii) on account of failure by her/person related to her to meet such demand.
25.

To prove the aforesaid, the prosecution has examined only four witnesses namely PW-2 Ms.
Jamuna, PW-5 Ms. Premwati, PW-6 Mr. Bablu and PW-7 Mr. Rajesh, who are the mother and siblings of deceased Ms. Neelam.
They are the only material witnesses examined by the prosecution in the present case.
Besides the aforesaid witnesses, the prosecution had also cited one Mr. Anil Kumar, S/o Sh. Bhagwan Singh, who was brother of the deceased, in the list of prosecution witnesses.

The said witness PW Mr. Anil had been dropped as a witness vide statement of the learned Additional Public Prosecutor for the State recorded on 07.08.2019.
26.
Accordingly, it is the testimony of PW-2 Ms. Jamuna, PW-5 Ms. Premwati, PW-6 Mr. Bablu and PW-7 Mr. Rajesh which is required to be examined for determining the aforesaid aspects.
(a) Whether there was an unlawful demand for any property or valuable security by the accused Jitender Gahlot from the deceased Ms. Neelam or any person related to her?

27.1 In this regard, it is alleged in the statement of the complainant Ex.PW5/A that despite a sum of Rs.60,000/- to Rs.70,000/- having been given to the accused as dowry, by the family of the deceased Ms. Neelam, accused Jitender Gahlot, his sister and brother-in- law had expressed their dissatisfaction to the complainant regarding the dowry given by her in the marriage of the deceased.

There is no State Vs. Jitender Gahlot allegation whatsoever regarding any unlawful demand by the accused Jitender Gahlot or any of his relatives, in the complainant's statement Ex.PW5/A. 27.2 In the statement of Ms. Jamuna , sister of deceased Neelam, Ex.PW2/A, it is alleged that when accused Jitender Gahlot visited them in the village for the second time, he demanded a ring, chain and an Apache bike.
It is further alleged therein that accused told them that if they cannot fulfill his demands, they should transfer the house in his name, otherwise, he would continue to harass Neelam by beating her.
It is alleged therein that sufficient dowry had been given at the time of the marriage of the deceased Ms. Neelam.

6 27.3

In the statement of Mr. Bablu, brother of deceased Neelam, Ex.PW6/A, it is alleged that when his mother-in-law was unwell, accused Jitender Gahlot had gone to his in-laws' house at Tuglakabad Extension with them and at that time, accused Jitender Gahlot had demanded Rs.2,00,000/- from them.
He further stated that he had told accused Jitender Gahlot that they will pay the amount when their agricultural land is sold.
He added that he had also told the elder brother of accused Jitender Gahlot, namely, Mr. Krishan, that they will pay the amount once their agricultural land is sold.
27.4 In the statement of Mr. Rajesh, brother of deceased Neelam, Ex.PW7/A, there is no allegation regarding any unlawful demand by the accused Jitender Gahlot or his relatives.
In fact, in paragraph no. 7 thereof, it is specifically stated that there was no demand of dowry ever.
27.5 In the statement of Mr. Anil Kumar (brother of deceased) Ex.PW8/A, there is no allegation regarding any unlawful demand for State Vs. Jitender Gahlot dowry or valuable property.
In paragraph 6 of his statement, it is specifically stated that the witness Mr. Anil Kumar had no information regarding any demand of dowry having been made.

28. From the aforesaid statements of the mother and siblings of the deceased, on the basis of which the FIR was registered, the following allegations regarding unlawful demand(s) made by the accused Jitender Gahlot or his relatives can be culled out:
i.
During his second visit to the village of the deceased, accused Jitender Gahlot demanded a ring, chain and an Apache bike from the family of the deceased;

ii. During his second visit to the village of the deceased, accused Jitender Gahlot demanded that, in case they are unable to fulfill his aforesaid demand of a ring, chain and Apache bike, the family of the deceased should transfer their house in his name;
and iii.
During his visit to the house of the in-laws of Mr. Bablu at Tughlakabad, to see his ailing mother-in-law, accused Jitender Gahlot demanded Rs.2,00,000/- from Mr. Bablu.

29.1 As regards the first of the aforesaid three demands, viz. demand of ring, chain and Apache bike,
it is pertinent to note that neither any date or time nor the exact place of making of the said demand has been specified either in the statement Ex.PW2/A of Ms. Jamuna or her statement under Section 161 Cr.P.C.

Further, the remaining material witnesses, including PW-5 Ms. Premwati who admittedly resided in the village, where the alleged demand is stated to have been made, have not supported the said allegation regarding demand of a ring, chain and Apache bike in their statements Ex.PW5/A, State Vs. Jitender Gahlot Ex.PW6/A, Ex.PW7/A and Ex.PW8/A or even their statements under Section 161 Cr.P.C.
29.2

In her testimony as PW-2, Ms. Jamuna has deposed that while no dowry demand was made at the time of marriage of her sister Neelam, during his second visit to their village with deceased Neelam, the accused Jitender had demanded vehicle and gold ring from them.
PW-2 has not supported her own allegations regarding demand of chain by the accused Jitender.

Further, though in her statement Ex.PW2/A, she had alleged that an Apache bike had been demanded by the State vs Jitender Gahlot on 10 November, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/170232380/
7 accused, in her testimony, PW-2 has not specified the vehicle, let alone the make thereof, which was allegedly demanded by accused Jitender Gahlot.

Further, while in her testimony, PW-2 has stated that accused Jitender Gahlot had demanded a gold ring, in her statement Ex.PW2/A, Ms. Jamuna has, however, not specified if the ring allegedly demanded by the accused was a gold ring.
The same is an improvement in the testimony of PW-2.
In her cross-examination, PW-2 Ms. Jamuna has specifically stated that she did not remember the dates when her sister Neelam had visited their native village after her marriage.
However, she stated that Neelam had visited twice.
The accused and deceased had been married for less than six months.
Considering the short length of the relationship, if not the exact dates, the witness could at least have stated the month(s) of the alleged visit(s), especially the one later in point of time.
However, she has merely stated that the said demand was made during the second visit.
Thus, the testimony of PW-2 Ms. Jamuna is not found to be sufficient or reliable to prove the first of the aforesaid demands allegedly made by the accused.
State Vs. Jitender Gahlot 29.3

While PW-2 has stated in her cross-examination that at that time, she and her mother were present at the house, her mother PW-5 Ms. Premwati has not uttered a word regarding any visit of the deceased, with or without the accused, to her village residence after the marriage of the deceased, let alone any demand of dowry having been made by the accused Jitender as alleged by PW-2 to have been made by the accused in the presence of PW-5.

Further, the remaining material witnesses namely PW-6 Mr. Bablu and PW-7 Mr. Rajesh have also not supported the allegation regarding demand of ring, chain and Apache bike in their testimonies recorded in the court.
29.4 Accordingly, the first alleged demand, viz. demand of ring, chain and Apache bike by the accused Jitender Gahlot, has not been proved by the prosecution.

30.1 As regards the second of the aforesaid demands, viz. demand regarding transfer of house in name of the accused, it is pertinent to note that neither any date or time nor the exact place of making of the said demand has been specified either in the statement Ex.PW2/A of Ms. Jamuna or her statement under Section 161 Cr.P.C.

Further, the remaining material witnesses, including PW-5 Ms. Premwati who admittedly resided in the village, where the alleged demand is stated to have been made, have not supported the said demand in their statements Ex.PW5/A, Ex.PW6/A,
Ex.PW7/A and Ex.PW8/A or even their statements under Section 161 Cr.P.C.
30.2

In her testimony as PW-2, Ms. Jamuna has deposed that during his second visit to their village with deceased Neelam, when she told the accused Jitender that they were not in a position to fulfill his State Vs. Jitender Gahlot demand of vehicle and gold ring as they had already given dowry articles at the time of marriage and her father had already expired
, accused Jitender told them that if they are unable to fulfill his demand, they should transfer their house in his name.
However, in her testimony, PW-2 has not mentioned the date and time or exact place of making of the said demand by the accused.

In fact, in her cross-examination, she has specifically stated that she does not remember the dates when her sister Neelam had visited their native village after her marriage but clarified that she had visited twice.

Considering the short length of marital relationship between the accused and the deceased, i.e. about 6 months, the witness could at least have mentioned the month, if not the exact date(s) of the alleged visit, which was allegedly the second visit and, thus,
State vs Jitender Gahlot on 10 November, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/170232380/
8 later in point of time.
She has further not stated as to whether the alleged demand was made inside their house or elsewhere in their village.
PW-2 has not even specified the particulars of the house of which the accused had allegedly demanded transfer in his favour.

In the absence of the said particulars, the alleged demand regarding transfer of house in favour of the accused cannot be said to have been proved through the testimony of PW-2.
30.3
None of the other material witnesses have deposed regarding the alleged demand regarding transfer of house in favour of accused.

While according to PW-2, her mother was also present at the house when the accused had visited them in the village along with the deceased, the testimony of PW-5 Ms. Premwati is silent with regard to any such demand having been made by the accused in her presence.

Further, the remaining material witnesses viz. PW-6 Mr. Bablu and PW- 7 Mr. Rajesh have also not supported the allegations regarding demand State Vs. Jitender Gahlot of transfer of house in favour of accused.
30.4 Thus, the alleged second demand regarding transfer of house in favour of accused has not been proved by the prosecution.

31.1 As regards the third alleged demand of Rs. 2 Lacs from the brother of deceased, namely, Mr.
Bablu Kumar, it is noteworthy that while in the statement Ex. PW-6/A, PW Mr. Bablu Kumar has stated that the same was made by the accused at the residence of the mother- in-law of PW-6 Mr.
Bablu Kumar at Tuglakabad Extension, neither the date and time nor the exact address of the aforesaid house have been mentioned therein.
The said details do not find mention even in the statement under Section 161 Cr.P.C of PW-6 Mr. Bablu Kumar.
Therefore, the aforesaid allegation of demand of dowry is devoid of material particulars.

Further, the remaining material witnesses have not supported the said demand in their statements Ex.PW2/A, Ex.PW5/A, Ex.PW7/A and Ex.PW8/A or even their statements under Section 161 Cr.P.C.
31.2

In his testimony as PW-6, Mr. Bablu Kumar has deposed that at the house of his in-laws, where he along with his sister Neelam and accused Jitender had gone as his mother-in-law was not feeling well, the accused had demanded Rs. 2 Lacs from him.
Like in his statement Ex. PW-6/A, in his testimony recorded in the court as well, PW-6 did not state the exact date or time of the alleged demand or visit to the house of his in-laws.

In fact, in response to a specific question on this aspect during cross-examination by the learned counsel for the accused, PW-6 stated that he did not remember as to when he had received the call from the house of his in-laws about the illness of his State Vs. Jitender Gahlot mother-in-law.
Therefore, PW-6 could not tell the date of the alleged visit to the house of his in-laws even upon cross-examination.
Interestingly, there is contradiction in the statement Ex. PW-6/A and the testimony of PW-6 with regard to the chronology of events and consequently the time period when the alleged demand was made.

In his statement Ex. PW-6/A,
Mr. Bablu has stated in paragraph 5 that the accused had demanded Rs. 2 Lacs from him and thereafter, in paragraph 6, he has stated that he had received a phone call from his sister Neelam.

However, in his examination-in-chief, PW-6 Mr. Bablu has deposed in paragraph 1 thereof that one month prior to her death, his sister Neelam had told him that her husband used to torture her for demand of dowry/money and in paragraph 2 he has deposed that "after sometime"

9
his mother-in-law was not feeling well and he along with his sister Neelam and accused Jitender had gone to the house of his in-laws where the accused had demanded Rs. 2 Lacs from him.

Accordingly, while from the statement Ex. PW6/A, it appears that the aforesaid alleged demand was made by the accused prior to the phone call made by the deceased to PW-6 informing him about beatings given to her by the accused, in his testimony, PW-6 has stated that the demand was made after some time of the aforesaid alleged phone call made by the deceased to him about one month prior to her death.
There is accordingly an apparent contradiction as to when the alleged demand was made by the accused.
Further, in his testimony, PW-6 did not even mention the State, city or locality where the house of his in-laws was situated, let alone specifying the exact address thereof.

Moreover, while in his testimony, PW-6 has mentioned that his sister Neelam had also accompanied him and the accused Jitender to the house of his in-laws State Vs. Jitender Gahlot when his mother-in-law was unwell, his statement Ex. PW6/A does not mention that deceased Neelam had also gone to the house of the in-laws of PW-6.
Thus, there are deficiencies as well as inconsistencies and contradictions in the various versions of PW-6 Mr. Bablu with regard to the alleged demand of Rs. 2 Lacs made by the accused Jitender.

31.3 The testimonies of the remaining material witnesses namely PW-2 Ms. Jamuna,
PW-5 Ms. Premwati and PW-7 Mr. Rajesh are silent with regard to the alleged demand of Rs. 2 Lacs by the accused.
31.4 Accordingly, the prosecution has not been able to establish that the accused Jitender Gahlot had demanded Rs. 2 Lacs from Mr. Bablu, brother of deceased, as dowry, as alleged.

32. Besides, the aforesaid three demands appearing in the statements of the relatives of the deceased recorded during investigation, yet another demand has been alleged to have been made by the accused, by PW-2 Ms. Jamuna in her cross-examination.
PW-2 has therein alleged that the accused had demanded a share in their agricultural land when quarrel took place with him.

However, the said alleged demand is also devoid of material particulars, such as date, time and place when the same was made,
as also the person(s) in whose presence it was made.

Even otherwise, the said demand has for the first time been alleged in the cross-examination of PW-2 and is,
therefore, in the nature of an after-thought and improvement.

The said demand has also not been supported by the remaining material witnesses viz. PW-5 Ms.
Premwati, PW-6 Mr. Bablu Kumar and PW-7 Mr. Rajesh.

The case of the prosecution is that the accused Jitender Gahlot, who was married to the complainant's daughter Ms. Neelam (since deceased) on 31.07.2017, subjected her (deceased Neelam) to cruelty and harassment for not meeting his unlawful demand of dowry, including soon before her death; and that on 24.01.2018, i.e. within seven years of her marriage, at G-38, Gali no. 2,
Som Bazar Road, Rajapuri, Uttam Nagar, New Delhi, Ms. Neelam died otherwise than under normal circumstances.
The spot was got inspected through the Crime Team and the concerned Executive Magistrate was informed.
The dead body was shifted to Deen Dayal Upadhyay Hospital, Delhi, where the patient was declared brought dead on examination vide MLC No. 23542.
The hanging material, i.e. chunni of the deceased, was seized.
Thereafter, the body was handed over to its relatives.
On 01.02.2018, the Executive Magistrate directed the SHO to take necessary action as per law, pursuant to which, the instant FIR was registered under Section 498A/304B IPC and investigation was handed over to Inspector Narender Singh.
The FSL report and subsequent opinion regarding manner of death were filed through a supplementary charge-sheet.
In light of the police report and the documents filed alongwith the same, the learned Metropolitan Magistrate took cognizance vide order dated 01.05.2018.

vide order dated 24.05.2018, committed the case for trial to the Court of Sessions.

opennyai_summary.issue:
In order to bring home the guilt of the accused in respect of State Vs. Jitender Gahlot the offence punishable under Section 498A I.P.C., the prosecution was required to prove the following:
(i) that the accused was the husband of the deceased Ms. Neelam; and (ii) that the accused had subjected the deceased Ms. Neelam to cruelty.

Neelam?

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
The prosecution has,
therefore, proved that the accused Jitender Gahlot was State Vs. Jitender Gahlot the husband of the deceased.
The term "cruelty" has been defined in the Explanation1 to Section 498A I.P.C.
In the instant case, the prosecution has pressed clause (b) thereof into service.
It has been alleged that the accused Jitender Gahlot had harassed the deceased Ms. Neelam with a view to coerce her or her parents/family to meet unlawful demand for property/valuable security or on account of failure by her or her family to meet such demand.
Thus, in order to establish the charge under Section 498A IPC against the accused Jitender Gahlot, the prosecution was required to prove beyond reasonable doubt that during the subsistence of marriage accused Jitender Gahlot with the deceased Ms.
Neelam, the accused Jitender Gahlot subjected the deceased to harassment in relation to non-fulfillment of his demands for dowry.
For that purpose, the prosecution was required to prove the following:
(a) that there was an unlawful demand for any property or valuable security by the accused Jitender Gahlot from the deceased or any person related to her;
(b) that the accused Jitender Gahlot harassed the deceased Ms. Neelam; and 1 Explanation to Section 498A IPC reads as under:-

Thus, the testimony of PW-2 Ms. Jamuna is not found to be sufficient or reliable to prove the first of the aforesaid demands allegedly made by the accused.
The said allegation is not only hearsay but also devoid of material particulars regarding date, time and place.
, his State Vs. Jitender Gahlot testimony is completely silent as to the steps, if any, taken by him pursuant to the aforesaid cries or phone call(s) made by the deceased to him.
The same compels this court to conclude that the witness PW-6 did not take any steps or act upon the cries for help made by the deceased.
Such conduct on part of a brother is unnatural.
Even otherwise, the said allegation contained in the statement Ex.PW7/A is devoid of material particulars such as date, time and place of alleged beatings and the manner in which the witness PW-7 acquired knowledge of the alleged quarrel between the accused and the deceased or beatings given by the accused to the deceased.
40.5 There is no other allegation regarding any harassment of the deceased by the accused in the testimony of PW-7.
In view of the aforesaid, the testimony of PW-7 Mr. Rajesh does not help the prosecution in establishing that the accused Jitender had ever harassed the deceased Ms. Neelam.
40.6 In view of the aforesaid, the prosecution has failed to prove that the accused Jitender had ever harassed the deceased Neelam.
41. Since the prosecution has not been able to prove that there was any unlawful demand for any property or valuable security from the deceased Ms. Neelam or any person related to her or that the accused Jitender Gahlot harassed the deceased Ms. Neelam, there is no need to dwell upon whether there was any harassment in relation to a demand of dowry or non-fulfillment thereof.
42. In view of the above discussion, the prosecution has failed to establish that the accused Jitender Gahlot had subjected the deceased Ms. Neelam to cruelty as alleged.
Accordingly, the said ingredient of the offence punishable under Section 498A IPC has not been established by the prosecution.
43. In light of the above, the prosecution has failed to prove the guilt of the accused Jitender Gahlot in respect of the offence punishable under Section 498A I.P.C.
II. Charge for the offence punishable under Section 304 B IPC 44.
To establish the charge in respect of the offence punishable under Section 304B2 IPC against the accused Jitender Gahlot, it was 2 Section 304-B of the Indian Penal Code reads as under:-

15 (1) Where the death of a woman is caused by any burns or bodily injury or occurs otherwise than under normal circumstances within seven years of her marriage and it is shown that soon before her death she was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or any relative of her husband for or in connection with, any demand for dowry, such death shall be called "dowry death", and such husband or relative shall be deemed to have caused her death".
State Vs. Jitender Gahlot 24.01.2018.
Thus, the accused has not disputed the fact that his wife Neelam had been found dead in her house/room.
In order to prove the aforesaid, the prosecution was required to examine the said persons who had seen the deceased Neelam hanging by the ceiling fan with a chunni and had removed her body from the ceiling fan and placed it on the cot.
Since as per the case of prosecution, the body of the deceased had already been removed from the ceiling fan and placed on a cot, by neighbours and sister of the accused, before arrival of the first investigating officer at the spot, there are no photographs to show that the deceased was hanging by the ceiling fan with a chunni wrapped around her neck at one end and the ceiling fan at the other end.
Thus, the prosecution has failed to prove the circumstances that the deceased Ms. Neelam was found hanging by the ceiling fan with a chunni on the fateful day.
The same is a serious lapse on part of the prosecution in establishing the circumstances around the death of the deceased Ms. Neelam.
Based on the post mortem report and the testimony of the concerned doctor PW-11 Dr. Neeraj Kumar Garg, it can safely be concluded that the death of Ms. Neelam in the instant case was caused otherwise than under normal circumstances.
50. Thus, while the prosecution has not been able to establish the entire chain of circumstances surrounding the death of Ms. Neelam, it has through the medical and other evidence on record successfully established that the daughter of the complainant, namely, Ms. Neelam had died on 24.01.2018 and that her death had been caused othwewise than under normal circumstances.
Thus, the prosectuion has successfully established that the death of Ms. Neelam had occurred within seven years of her marriage.
any cruelty or harassment was meted out to deceased Ms. Neelam by accused Jitender Gahlot at any point during the subsistence of their marriage.
there was any unlawful demand for any property or dowry by the accused Jitender Gahlot or his relatives from the deceased Ms. Neelam or her relatives.
As has already been discussed above, the prosecution has failed to establish that the accused Jitender Gahlot had at any point of time subjected the deceased Ms. Neelam to cruelty or harassment.
Accordingly, the question of cruelty or harassment having been meted out to her soon before her death does not arise.
57. Prosecution has failed to establish that after marriage of deceased, there were circumstances of harassment or cruelty that took place on account of demand of dowry which could connect with death of State Vs. Jitender Gahlot deceased.
Therefore, the aforesaid ingredient of the offence punishable under Section 304 B IPC has also not been proved by the prosecution.
58. Presumption under Section 113B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 can be drawn only where ingredients of Section 304B of IPC are fulfilled.
Prosecution has failed to prove the chain of necessary ingredients to raise the presumption under Section 113B of the Indian Evidence Act.
59 . Therefore, the prosecution has also failed to prove the guilt of the accused Jitender Gahlot in respect of the offence punishable under Section 304 B I.P.C.
CONCLUSION 60.
In view of the above discussion, in the considered opinion of this Court, the prosecution has miserably failed to prove its case against the accused.
